contract_plain_english: For one-dimensional conservation laws, the rate of change of the conserved quantity in a spatial interval equals the flux at its first endpoint minus the flux at its second endpoint (printed p. 4, (1.10)). If the state q and composed flux f(q) are sufficiently smooth, this integral law yields the differential conservation equation (printed p. 4, Section 1.1.2). Interesting solutions can contain discontinuities, and nonlinear conservation laws can develop them even from smooth initial data (printed pp. 4–5, Section 1.1.2). At such a discontinuity, the differential equation does not hold classically, while the integral conservation law remains the fundamental equation that continues to hold for these solutions (printed p. 5, Section 1.1.2). The supplied passage leaves the precise solution class, endpoint conventions, and temporal interpretation of the integral balance unspecified.
